title: add, sub, inc, dec and neg
summary: add and sub combine two operands into the first, inc and dec add or take away one, and neg flips the sign. Results wrap around at the register's size, so 32-bit arithmetic wraps at 2 to the 32 and also clears the upper half. The same add instruction serves signed and unsigned numbers, because two's complement makes them the same bits.
markdown:
## Two operands, one result

x86 arithmetic overwrites its first operand:

| Instruction | Does |
|---|---|
| `add rax, rbx` | rax = rax + rbx |
| `sub rax, 5` | rax = rax − 5 |
| `inc rcx` | rcx = rcx + 1 |
| `dec rcx` | rcx = rcx − 1 |
| `neg rax` | rax = −rax |

There is no "c = a + b" in one instruction (except with `lea`, lesson 4.01): copy first, then add.

```nasm
        global  _start
        section .text
_start:
        mov     rbx, 1000
        mov     rax, rbx
        add     rax, 337        ; rax = 1337
        sub     rax, 1300       ; rax = 37
        inc     rax             ; 38
        dec     rbx             ; rbx = 999
        neg     rbx             ; -999
        add     rax, rbx        ; 38 - 999 = -961
        mov     rdi, rax
        call    print_int
        call    print_newline
        mov     eax, 60
        xor     edi, edi
        syscall
```

## Wrapping around

A register has a fixed number of bits, so results wrap around like a car's odometer. With 8 bits, 255 + 1 is 0; with 64 bits, the biggest unsigned number plus one is 0 too.

```demo-asm
title: Wrapping at 8, 32 and 64 bits
init: rax=0
    mov al, 255
    add al, 1
    mov eax, 0xFFFFFFFF
    add eax, 1
    mov rax, -1
    add rax, 1
    ret
```

Watch the **CF** (carry) flag in the demo: it is set each time a result wrapped past the top. Lesson 2.04 is about the flags.

> [!tip] 32-bit arithmetic clears the top too
> Like `mov`, any instruction writing a 32-bit register zeroes the upper half. `add eax, 1` with `rax = 0x1_FFFFFFFF` gives `rax = 0`, not `0x2_00000000`. Use 64-bit registers when numbers can grow beyond about 4 billion.

## One add for signed and unsigned

In two's complement (from the Fundamentals course), −1 is all 1 bits. Adding 1 to it gives all 0 bits: 0, which is right whether you read the bits as signed (−1 + 1) or unsigned (the largest value + 1, wrapping). That is the beauty of two's complement: **the same `add` and `sub` work for both**. Only comparisons, division and widening need to know which you mean.

## Instructions with memory

Arithmetic can read or update memory directly (lesson 4.01 shows addressing):

```nasm-norun
        add     rax, [rel total]        ; rax += the 8 bytes at total
        add     qword [rel total], 5    ; the 8 bytes at total += 5
        inc     dword [rel count]       ; the 4 bytes at count += 1
```

When neither operand is a register, NASM cannot tell the size, so you write it: `byte`, `word`, `dword` or `qword`. Only one operand may be in memory: `add [a], [b]` does not exist.

## Check yourself
```quiz
? What does sub rax, rbx do?
- rbx = rbx - rax
- rax = rbx - rax
+ rax = rax - rbx
> The first operand is the destination.

? al is 250. After add al, 10, what is al?
- 260
+ 4
- 255
> 260 wraps around at 256.

? Why can the same add instruction handle signed and unsigned numbers?
- add checks the sign first
+ In two's complement both give the same bits
- It cannot: there is a separate signed add
> Comparisons and division are where the difference matters.

? What is wrong with inc [rel count]?
- inc cannot use a memory operand
- Nothing: it assembles as it is
+ The size is unknown; write `dword` or another size
> With no register in the instruction, NASM cannot tell how many bytes to change, so write `inc dword [rel count]`.
```
